stories.title: Labour will not have the courage to cut spending, says Badenoch
stories.summary: Speaking ahead of next week's Budget, the Conservative leader says her party would make £70bn of cuts.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 20 October 2026

Kemi Badenoch has said Labour will not have the "courage" to make the public spending cuts she argued were necessary to bring down debt and fund defence.

Speaking in central London, the Conservative leader said the chancellor was hoping to deliver a "nothing to see here Budget" next week but added: "Britain cannot afford to do as little as possible."

Highlighting her own plans to reduce spending by £70bn, Badenoch said: "Cuts are never easy but they are much easier to accept if what you are doing is fair."

Labour Party chairwoman Bridget Phillipson described Badenoch's solution as "reverse Robin Hood politics – giving tax breaks to the wealthiest while offering nothing to ordinary people".

Chancellor John Healey is due to set out his tax and spending plans on 28 October - the first Budget since Andy Burnham became prime minister.

Healey has come under pressure to set out how he will boost defence funding to 3% of national income by 2030. However, this announcement is not expected until the government's spending review next year.

The Budget is also unlikely to include details about any changes to the welfare system, with those expected once former cabinet minister Alan Milburn produces his review into young people and work.

Badenoch said: "If Labour's plan is to kick tough decisions into the long grass, come out with tiny bits of micro-policy, put up a few taxes, spend a bit more on welfare, and hope nobody notices before the next election, they are kidding themselves."

The Tory leader noted that the International Monetary Fund (IMF) had recently praised the UK for its plans to reduce its borrowing.

"The IMF clearly don't know this Labour Party like I do," she said.

She said Labour's plans required "huge cuts to the public sector" in 2029 and that the party would call an election before then.

"They are not suddenly going to find the courage to cut spending in the final year of a Parliament right before an election... Investors aren't buying these fictional cuts either."

Unexpected UK borrowing surge adds to pre-Budget pressure on chancellor Published 22 September

Banks expect to be hit with higher taxes in Budget Published 4 days ago

What is the Budget and what could be in it? Published 20 hours ago

The most recent figures show that in August government borrowing stood at £18.3bn. The government is paying £8.8bn on its debt - the highest level since records began in 1997.

Badenoch said her party would reduce borrowing by finding £70bn of savings, including through cuts to the welfare bill.

Under her party's "golden economic rule", half of the savings would go towards reducing the deficit.

"Cuts are never easy, but they are much easier to accept if what you are doing is fair," she said.

"Fair to taxpayers, fair to future generations, and fair to those who really do need support."

The Conservatives have recently announced they would scrap inheritance tax on family homes and allow couples to leave £1m tax-free.

The party has also pledged to scrap a rule that sees parents in England earning more than £100,000 a year lose out on childcare support .

Asked if the Conservatives were the party for the rich, Badenoch told the BBC her policies would "help everyone".

"Quite frankly, getting people off welfare is doing something for them... the best welfare is a well-paying job," she said.

Pressed on whether she would make changes to the triple lock to reduce the amount spent on pensions, Badenoch said she did not want to see "pensioner poverty" and that there were other things the party could do to grow the economy.

The trade unions and the Liberal Democrats have urged the government to raise money by putting a windfall tax on banks, who have reported large profits in recent years.

Badenoch dismissed this suggestion, arguing it would hit bank shareholders, including people's pension funds.

Setting out her party's policy Liberal Democrat leader Daisy Cooper said: "It's outrageous that while households have been grappling with the cost-of-living crisis, the big banks have benefited from a taxpayer-funded windfall worth billions."

She said the money raised from putting higher taxes on the bank could go towards reducing the cost of petrol and diesel and transport fares.

Reform UK economic spokesman Robert Jenrick challenged Healey to use the Budget to increase funding for defence, reduce benefit fraud and to make cuts to "foreign aid to rich countries" and "all the mad net-zero subsidies".

Speaking at a Reform rally in Plymouth, Jenrick added: "I suspect he won't. In fact, I confidently predict that this Budget will contain exactly what the last two did: tax rises again."

Responding to Badenoch's speech, Phillipson said: "Under the Tories debt rocketed, interest rates went up, while family finances and businesses were hammered.

"Labour has taken the fair decisions to reverse the Conservatives' decline. The economy is growing, interest rates have fallen, and private investment has returned.

"We're giving people breathing space on the cost of living and delivering everyday fixes to make life that little bit easier."

stories.title: Bereaved families could face 'unjust' tax bill after civil service pension delays
stories.summary: The chairman of Parliament's Public Accounts Committee says families should not be taxed through no fault of their own.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 19 October 2026

Bereaved families affected by severe delays paying out civil service pensions could face an "unjust" tax bill, the government has been warned.

Under HMRC rules, certain lump sum pension payments must be paid within two years of the pension scheme being notified of a death to remain tax-free.

Conservative MP Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, who chairs Parliament's Public Accounts Committee, said it was "unconscionable" some families could face a "death tax" through no fault of their own.

The Cabinet Office said that if delays caused a tax charge there were existing avenues to claim compensation, such as the Pensions Ombudsman.

However, the ombudsman is currently advising that standard complaints are only likely to be resolved within 18 months, with more complex cases facing a longer wait.

The Civil Service Pension scheme manages the pensions of 1.7 million public sector workers in the UK.

Outsourcing firm Capita took over the administration of the scheme from a company called MyCSP in December 2025, saying it inherited a backlog of more than 86,000 cases.

Despite a two-year transition period to prepare for the takeover, problems have persisted and by February the backlog had grown to 120,000 cases.

Retired civil servants and bereaved families have been left waiting months for pension payments, with some struggling to pay bills.

Civil service pension backlog 'overwhelmed' Capita, boss says Published 12 February

Emergency loans offered to civil servants waiting on pensions Published 29 January

Retired civil servants left in pension limbo Published 23 January

According to the latest figures up to 30 September , external , 1,643 outstanding cases of bereavement or death in service are more than 100 days old.

Of these, only 301 are in scope to be paid within 15 days.

The PCS union, which represents civil servants, said that while not all these cases would ultimately be affected by the two-year tax rule, there were "serious questions" over how long they would remain unresolved.

The Cabinet Office said that while the number of individuals approaching the two-year threshold was currently fewer than 10, "we are treating every case with urgency".

If someone dies before the age of 75, a pension lump sum death benefit is only tax-free if it is paid within two years of the pension scheme first becoming aware of the death, and if the value is below the deceased's Lump Sum and Death Benefit Allowance.

The payment would be taxed at the same rate as the beneficiary's income tax rate.

Sir Geoffrey has written to Cabinet Office Minister Louise Haigh to urge the government to confirm the bereaved families affected will not face this "unjust financial penalty".

His letter came after BBC Radio 4's Money Box Live highlighted the potential tax liability.

Sir Geoffrey said "the chaos currently engulfing the Civil Service Pension Scheme means that the likelihood of death benefit payments being made within two years is slim".

He warned "a significant number" of family members "will be watching the clock quickly tick down to a year, as the maladministration of the scheme enters its tenth month".

He added: "This is an additional stress they should not have to bear."

Writing in response to Sir Geoffrey's letter, Minister Sally Jameson said neither the Cabinet Office nor the pension scheme administrator had the power under tax law to alter or waive these tax charges.

However, she said where delays lead to an avoidable tax charge people "will not be left out of pocket" and the pension scheme "will ensure compensation is processed swiftly".

She added that the Cabinet Office was working with Capita to ensure the oldest outstanding cases were prioritised.

Money Box Live: Capita, What Went Wrong?

Money Box Live looks at what is going on with Capita, which administers millions of people's pensions

Rob Wassell, 58, has been waiting almost two years for the lump sum from his brother's civil service pension, following his death.

On 22 October it will be two years since the pension scheme was notified of his death so if he does not receive the payment in just a few days times, it could face being taxed.

Rob, who contacted the BBC's Money Box programme about his case, said he had been phoning Capita with increasing "desperation" as his situation dragged on.

"It's a bitter pill to swallow to have to pay tax for something which was not my fault," he said.

"It creates unnecessary worry and anguish through the process, which is already in itself difficult."

Rob said he needed the money to cover the estate costs he had to pay for his brother and fill a £20,000 hole in his savings.

However, he said it was "heartbreaking" to hear of other cases where people needed the money just to survive.

Rob added that the idea that he might face "another battle" to recoup the tax through compensation made it feel like "you just want to give up".

Rob has been waiting almost two years for the lump sum from his brother's civil service pension

Fran Heathcote, head of the PCS union, said it would be "a profound injustice" if families faced a further financial penalty because of Capita's failures.

"If that does happen, the government should be ashamed that families are being made to pay the price for failures that are entirely outside their control," she said.

A spokesperson for the Cabinet Office, which has overall responsibility for the Civil Service Pension Scheme, said: "The service levels following the move to Capita have been completely unacceptable and we are committed to ensuring no member is left financially worse off.

"We are continuing to hold Capita to account, including holding back nearly £10m in payments, and are doing everything in our power to ensure that individuals do not experience delays.

"If delays cause a tax charge, existing avenues for complaints can provide financial redress or compensation to cover losses."

A Capita spokesperson said: "We are deeply sorry for the frustration that the administration of the Civil Service Pension Scheme has caused members and their families.

"Our teams are working tirelessly to resolve outstanding cases as quickly as possible, with particular focus on people who have been waiting the longest and those facing financial hardship or challenging personal circumstances."

stories.title: Burnham risks wrath of Commons Speaker for talking too much at PMQs
stories.summary: The prime minister takes longer than his predecessors to respond to questions from MPs, writes Matt Chorley.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 20 October 2026

Andy Burnham has only been prime minister for three months, but he is already in trouble with the Commons Speaker for talking too much.

During the first three sessions of Prime Minister's Questions with Burnham at the despatch box, Sir Lindsay Hoyle has made repeated appeals for brevity.

But is he really any more verbose than his predecessors like Sir Keir Starmer, Rishi Sunak, Liz Truss and Boris Johnson?

Armed with a stopwatch for a dive into the archive, I've found that the new prime minister does seem to give fuller, longer answers – by some margin.

The weekly session of PMQs is scheduled to start at midday on Wednesdays when the Commons is sitting, and last for 30 minutes. However it routinely runs for 10, 15, even 20 minutes longer. And that has caused problems.

Burnham's PMQs debut shows the challenge of delivering new style of politics Published 2 September

" Can I just say I admire the prime minister?" Sir Lindsay said during Burnham's first PMQs.

"At least he's answering detailed questions. My problem is I'm not going to get through the list, and both of us will be in trouble with the backbenches when we don't make it."

Just last week he complained again: "We really are going to have to try and speed up some of the answers."

Based on an average of his first three times taking PMQs, Burnham has spoken for a total of 22 minutes per session. That's between three and six minutes more than the average for the other PMs I looked at each over three similar autumn sessions.

The number of questions asked each week can differ though, in part because time is running out. So I looked at the average time spent on each answer,

Of those I looked at, Truss was the fastest - averaging just 33 seconds per answer, followed by Johnson on 35 seconds, Sir Keir on 38 seconds and Sunak on 39 seconds.

By contrast Burnham was an outlier, taking on average 51 seconds per answer.

That means he talks for a third more per question than Sir Keir and Sunak, and up to 50% more than Truss.

Obviously the quantity of words is easier to assess than the quality.

Number 10 thinks there is a simple reason why the current PM takes longer than his predecessors. A senior source tells me: "It's because he actually answers the questions."

A spokesman for the speaker said: "The speaker is always keen to get in as many backbenchers as possible for any question session."

Listen to Matt Chorley weekdays from 14:00 on BBC Radio 5 Live and on the Urgent Questions podcast .

stories.title: Chancellor rejects calls to raise Capital Gains Tax in Budget
stories.summary: Influential Labour figures had been pushing for equalising CGT and income tax, but critics have said this could drive wealthy people out of Britain.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Chancellor John Healey says he wants to avoid an investor exodus from the UK

Published 20 October 2026

Chancellor John Healey has dismissed calls from some Labour MPs to increase Capital Gains Tax (CGT).

Cabinet ministers Wes Streeting and Louise Haigh both previously voiced support for raising CGT before Andy Burnham became prime minister in July.

Ahead of next week's Budget, as first reported by the Times , external , Healey is minded not to increase CGT - which is imposed on the profit people make when they sell an asset that has increased in value, such as shares in a company or properties which are not primary residences.

The move followed warnings that it could end up costing the government money if wealthy people leave the country or defer selling off assets.

If you pay income tax at the basic rate then CGT is charged at 18%. For higher and additional rate income tax payers, the CGT rate is 24%.

Last year, HMRC estimated , external that lifting the lower rate of CGT by 1% could raise £5m by 2028-9 but increasing the higher rate of CGT by 10% would reduce the Treasury's receipts by £3.6bn in 2028-9.

The amount raised could be reduced if people adapt their behaviour to the tax rise, for example by moving abroad or deciding not to sell a property.

The chancellor gave an indication of his approach last month in a speech when he spoke about the importance of businesses and self-employed people making profits.

"I want to see this country as a country of wealth creation. I want our government decisions and policies to raise the levels of confidence, and investment, and profit in British business," Healey said.

Burnham has faced warnings against lifting CGT. His former adviser and Goldman Sachs Chief Economist Lord Jim O'Neill suggested it would send "the wrong message to business".

But influential Labour figures had pushed for equalising CGT and income tax, with the former generally attracting a lower tax rate.

Louise Haigh, a key ally of the prime minister, had suggested capital gains should go up to be closer to income tax, before she became Burnham's first secretary of state.

In an article for the Renewal journal, , external Haigh argued that raising CGT would "shift the taxation burden away from punishing work, and towards unproductive capital accumulation which does little to grow the everyday economy".

She said this could be accompanied by measures to ensure that "genuine investment returns are not penalised".

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting called for a "wealth tax that works" in May, shortly after resigning as a minister in former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer's government.

He had argued that equalising CGT with income tax would address an unfair system that was "penalising work".

Healey had already ruled out levelling the two tax rates, according to a report in the Financial Times last week , external .

Asked about the government's plans for CGT on BBC Breakfast, Communities Secretary Angela Rayner would not speculate on the Budget.

Pressed over whether rejecting calls to increase the tax was a win for the rich, she said the government had already taken steps to give people "breathing space" and help with the cost of living.

It comes after senior banking executives told the BBC they expect Healey to raise taxes on the sector. UK banks have been reporting bumper profits, leading to calls from unions for higher taxes.

Healey is due to set out his tax and spending plans at his first Budget on 28 October, against the backdrop of the US-Iran war which has led to rising prices.

The chancellor is under pressure to find measures to ease the cost of living and fund an increase for defence at his spending review next year.

The chancellor's options for raising money are limited as Labour's 2024 manifesto pledged not to increase income tax, National Insurance and VAT, the three big revenue raisers.

The government is also restricted in how much it can borrow due to its self-imposed rules on debt.

What is the Budget and what could be in it? Published 20 hours ago

Labour will not have the courage to cut spending, says Badenoch Published 13 hours ago

Banks expect to be hit with higher taxes in Budget Published 4 days ago

In a pre-Budget speech on Tuesday, Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch urged the government to cut spending and reduce its borrowing.

She said the prime minister and the chancellor should "live within our means" and pointed to her party's plan to save £70bn in cuts, including to welfare and overseas development aid.

Badenoch told an audience in central London that Labour would not "find the courage" to cut spending.

She said the chancellor wanted to deliver a "nothing to see here Budget" but added: "Britain cannot afford to do as little as possible."

The Liberal Democrats have said the government could raise £14bn partly by introducing a windfall tax on the profits of banks.

The party's deputy leader Daisy Cooper said the money could go towards cutting fuel duty, rail and bus fares and VAT for hospitality businesses.

stories.title: Jobless rate falls but small firms cut back hiring
stories.summary: Small firms cite labour costs as a key factor in scaling back hiring, the Office for National Statistics says.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 20 October 2026

The UK's unemployment rate has dropped to its lowest for more than year, but job vacancies have continued to fall as smaller businesses cut back on recruitment, official figures indicate.

The jobless rate fell to 4.7% in the three months to August, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said, the lowest since July last year.

However, vacancies fell by 21,000 in the three months to September to 691,000, with the ONS saying small firms were citing labour costs as a key factor in scaling back hiring.

The figures are the last official snapshot of the jobs market before the Budget, and analysts said they indicated the jobs market was showing signs of recovery despite the weakness in hiring.

ONS deputy director of labour market statistics, David Freeman, said the labour market remained "broadly flat", with the latest data showing the employment rate edging up and "a small drop in unemployment".

"The number of workers on payroll remains slightly down over the same period, though data for the most recent month suggests that might be starting to level off," he said.

"The number of vacancies has seen its largest fall since the start of the year, concentrated mainly within smaller businesses, which cite increased labour costs as a key factor."

Energy costs have risen since the Iran war began, and companies have also said that increases in National Insurance and the minimum wage have made it more expensive to employ staff.

The number of job vacancies fell to its lowest level in more than five years, the figures indicated, with the largest decrease in construction jobs.

Average earnings excluding bonuses rose 3.7% in the three months to August, up from 3.5% last month. Taking inflation into account, wages grew 0.8% in real terms.

Pat McFadden, the Secretary of State for Work and Pensions, said the figures "show the resilience of our labour market" with the UK's employment rate "now the third highest in the G7, despite a backdrop of global uncertainty".

However, he said that "too many young people still find themselves locked out of employment".

The government is working with industry "to bring young people back into the labour market and prevent them from drifting into the welfare system", he added.

But Conservative shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said on X , external that "businesses can't afford to hire".

"This is what happens when you attack employers, tax jobs, and put up red tape," he said.

The latest ONS figures showed the unemployment rate for those aged 16 to 24 was 15.6% in the June to August quarter. While that was down from 16.4% in the March to May period, it was still higher than the rate of 14.6% seen in the June-to-August period last year.

Separate ONS figures have indicated that nearly one million young people in the UK are not in education, employment or training - or "Neet"

On Monday, Prime Minister Andy Burnham warned the UK faces an "economic catastrophe and moral failure" due to high levels of youth unemployment.

Ashley Webb, senior UK economist for Capital Economics, said the fall in the unemployment rate was "unexpected", and that it suggests the labour market "continues to recover".

But "with businesses' energy costs likely to fall only slowly, we still think hiring will stay subdued," he said.

Louise Murphy, senior economist at the Resolution Foundation, said the labour market "has performed poorly in recent years as the number of jobs has fallen and pay growth weakened".

But she added that the UK's "recent bout of economic resilience may finally be creating some green shoots", pointing to "rising employment levels and private sector wage growth stabilising".

The quality of ONS statistics has been criticised in recent years, with a review last year finding "deep seated" issues with the body .

The Labour Force Survey, which it uses to report payroll and employment figures, has suffered from low response rates.

In an update on Tuesday, the ONS said that response levels had improved, but that "some volatility" remained in the statistics.

stories.title: Burnham vows end to 'rip-off parking charges' under new rules
stories.summary: The changes come after concerns that penalties issued by private providers are too harsh and leave motorists unfairly punished.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Published 19 October 2026

Drivers will be given the right to challenge "rip-off" private parking charges and more grace when using private providers under new rules set out by Andy Burnham.

The prime minister announced the changes after concerns were raised that penalties issued by private providers were too harsh and left motorists unfairly punished.

The new rules include a cancellation of charges for honest mistakes such as stopping to check directions and for non-payment due to broken ticket machines. Drivers will also get a 10-minute window to leave a car park without facing a penalty.

Motoring groups welcomed the changes, but said more needed to be done to stop charges when the driver had done nothing wrong.

Private car parks are different to council-owned car parks and streets, but more tickets at private sites are now being issued than ever recorded.

According to RAC analysis of government data, some 17 million private parking tickets were issued in 2025-26, a 17% increase from a year earlier.

With each charge worth up to £100, the data suggests drivers could collectively face private parking charges worth more than £4.6m each day.

In one case, a woman was taken to court in a £1,906 claim after taking longer than five minutes to pay at a car park in Derby . The charge was eventually dropped .

"Being a few minutes late back to your car or typing one digit of your number plate wrong shouldn't end with a hefty fine landing on your doormat," said Burnham.

He added that such charges left "people feeling ripped off and out of pocket".

The new rules will give drivers:

A guaranteed five-minute period to decide whether to park

A 10-minute window to leave without facing a penalty

Cancellation of charges for issues drivers can't control, such as vehicle breakdowns in car parks

Cancellation of charges for honest mistakes such as stopping to check directions, as well as for medical emergencies or broken ticket machines

Maximum charges of £20 on appeal for slip-ups such as forgetting a parking permit, entering the wrong vehicle registration, or forgetting to confirm the registration in the machine when parking

A freeze on the maximum parking charge at £100, which is the same limit as the current private parking Code of Practice

The new code will apply in England, Scotland and Wales.

Operators who do not comply risk losing access to DVLA data, making it more difficult to pursue the car's owner even if they do issue a charge.

'I got fined £11k over a five-minute parking rule' Published 1 August 2024

Firm told to pay £10,240 in five-minute parking row Published 5 April 2025

'Increase trust'

The government's Private Parking Code of Practice has been seven years in the making.

In 2019, an act of Parliament was passed to create a code but the code was withdrawn in 2022, due to "resistance from the private parking industry", according to the RAC.

The current industry Code of Practice, created by the British Parking Association and the International Parking Community, was introduced in 2024 and updated last year after a review .

Angela Rayner, the Communities and Housing Secretary, told BBC Breakfast that parking "shouldn't be a way of making money".

Asked if the changes were an admission that motorists have been "ripped off" by parking companies for years, she said: "We're calling time on it. They have regulated themselves and they have their appeals process but we're giving it more meat now."

She said the current level of fine was a "proportionate response to when people don't follow the rules".

Derek Millard-Smith from the British Parking Association said the group welcomed the changes as it would "increase trust" and said "detterents work" when it came to questions over the cost of fines.

"We know dog fouling, rail fare dodging, littering - all those levels are around £100 or more because that is a level that is deemed sufficient to change behaviours."

'Work to do'

Both the AA and the RAC said the new code was a good first step but did not go far enough.

The AA said some drivers pay up even if they have done nothing wrong, just to avoid the hassle and over fears of legal action being taken against them.

"There is still a huge amount of work to do, such as tackling the scourge of debt recovery fees," added Jack Cousens, head of roads policy at the AA.

"Ultimately, we need to stop charges being issued in the first place, especially where the driver has done nothing wrong."

The RAC's head of policy, Simon Williams, called for the banning of debt recovery fees and said the current industry-run appeals bodies should be replaced by a single independent one.

The government said it would be consulting on the issue of debt recovery fees, as well as other recommendations from the Competition and Markets Authority.

stories.title: Criminals detained in hospital set to lose benefits
stories.summary: The families of the victims of Nottingham killer Valdo Calocane had been campaigning for the change.
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
To play this video you need to enable JavaScript in your browser.

This video can not be played

Emma Webber says hospital offenders claiming benefits is unjust for victims' families

Published 20 October 2026

Killers and serious sex offenders detained in hospital are among the criminals who will no longer receive benefits under proposals called for by victims' families.

Regulations due to be laid out in Parliament on Tuesday seek to end the "double provision" and prevent serious criminals receiving up to £800 a month in universal credit over several years.

Emma Webber, the mother of Barnaby Webber, who was stabbed to death by Valdo Calocane in Nottingham, before the killer was sentenced to a hospital order, said she would now "demand" ministers reallocate the funds, which she said was a "no-brainer".

The government said closing the loophole would save an estimated tens of millions of pounds a year.

The families of the victims of triple killer Valdo Calocane had been calling for his benefits to be stopped

The new regulations are expected to come into force early next year, subject to parliamentary approval.

Currently, serious criminals on hospital orders - where their bed and board is funded by the NHS - continue to receive any benefits they were paid on the outside.

Students Barnaby and Grace O'Malley-Kumar, and grandfather Ian Coates, were stabbed to death on 13 June 2023 by Calocane, who had been diagnosed with paranoid schizophrenia in 2020.

Calocane was convicted of manslaughter on the basis of diminished responsibility, and detained at a high-security hospital.

The parents of Barnaby and Grace met Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden to discuss the change on Monday.

Emma Webber said the move was "long overdue".

Barnaby Webber, Grace O'Malley-Kumar and Ian Coates were killed in the Nottingham attacks

Webber told the BBC it was "not an insignificant amount of money - but it is not just the money".

"These criminal patients, who have devastated lives as well as taken lives, [are] not only having their full bed and board and all of their care and rehabilitation provided for them, but also amassing a small fortune while they're inside," she said.

"The rest of us on the outside are desperately trying to survive and find a way forward in our lives."

Webber said she believed the funds should be directed to the victims of serious crime so families "are given the support and the advocacy they need".

She added when her son was killed, her family was allocated a support worker who had 50 other families to look after.

Webber said: "I beg and I plead, and - actually, I demand - ministers now consider the appropriate reuse of those funds."

Dr Sanjoy Kumar, Grace's father, said: "Our campaign has always been about accountability and fairness.

"Offenders with treatment orders already cost the taxpayer an enormous amount.

"On release, every offender gets help with housing and benefits.

"On the principle of fairness alone, we do not see why taxpayers should fund benefits while they are incarcerated."

Gogoa Lois Tape, 28, was also detained by hospital order after strangling his partner

The mother of Kennedi Westcarr-Sabaroche, who was killed by her partner Gogoa Lois Tape in Hackney, east London, in April 2024, also lobbied for benefits paid to offenders in psychiatric hospitals to stop.

Tape was given a hospital order, detaining him indefinitely after he pleaded guilty to manslaughter by reason of diminished responsibility.

Kennedi's mother Linda Westcarr said: "For many victims' families, the question of whether serious offenders should continue to receive benefits raises understandable concerns about fairness, accountability and the values we uphold as a society.

"In my view, this is not simply a question of policy, it is also a matter of moral responsibility and ensuring that the impact on victims and their families is properly recognised."

Kennedi Westcarr-Sabaroche was killed in April 2024

The government said the move followed engagement with victims' families and experts as part of its plan to "put fairness back of the heart of the welfare system".

McFadden said: "We said we'd act to tackle this gross unfairness and we're delivering on that promise.

"For too long these violent criminals have had their living costs paid by the taxpayer twice over, while their victims and families paid the price.

"That ends today, because victims and taxpayers deserve a system that is fair and supports only those who genuinely need it."

Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government Angela Rayner paid tribute to the families who had campaigned on the matter.

She added: "I'm aware the secretary of state has met with the families regarding this and was quite frankly astonished that the situation was as it was, and that these people were receiving benefits.

"That's why the secretary of state has taken this action and I welcome it."

She added the reallocation of funds was "something for the chancellor and secretary of state".

Shadow work and pensions secretary Helen Whately said: "Killers and rapists should not pocket benefits from a hospital bed.

"Labour has taken all year to stop a loophole it promised to close. And tens of millions saved barely makes a dent in the benefits bill Labour has let spiral out of control.

"The Conservatives would make universal credit a conditional, time-limited benefit, so taxpayers' money goes only to those who genuinely need it."

The proposed regulations apply to individuals subject to a Section 37 order under the Mental Health Act 1983, and a Section 57A order under the Criminal Procedure (Scotland) Act 1995.

The offences covered include manslaughter, attempted murder, wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm, rape, assault by penetration and rape of a child under 13.

Murder is not included, because a hospital order is not an available sentence for the offence.

The change in regulation is expected to affect about 2,500 offenders already in hospital and approximately 200 a year in future, the government said, with the full financial impact of the move due to be published as part of the 2026 Budget on 28 October.

stories.title: Track UK's latest migration numbers - net migration, visas, asylum and small boats
stories.summary: Use our interactive tracker to explore the latest migration statistics for the UK
stories.contentStatus: Freely readable article text extracted from publisher page
stories.body:
Track UK's latest migration numbers - net migration, visas, asylum and small boats

Published 27 November 2025

Updated 20 October 2026

UK net migration has dropped to the lowest level, outside of the Covid pandemic, since 2012.

How does that sit alongside other key migration measures, including asylum applications, small boat arrivals and visas granted?

Scroll down to find out more about the latest key figures, and get answers to key questions on a range of topics.

UK migration data at a glance

Net migration (change in population), January 2025 to December 2025

Immigration (people arriving), January 2025 to December 2025

Emigration (people leaving), January 2025 to December 2025

Asylum applications, July 2025 to June 2026

Returns and deportations from the UK, July 2025 to June 2026

Arrivals by small boat, 1 January 2026 to 18 October 2026

Small boat crossings and other illegal arrivals

Between 1 January and 18 October 2026, a total of 20,935 people crossed the English Channel by small boat from France. This was down by 43% on the same period the previous year.

These crossings have become the most common way for people to be detected entering the UK illegally since 2020.

Nearly all those who arrive by small boat claim asylum. Under international law, this means they are allowed to stay in the country while their asylum application is considered.

Small boat arrivals made up 40% of asylum applications between July 2025 to June 2026.

Boats that arrived in the UK from 19 October 2025 to 18 October 2026 carried an average of 68 people. This has more than doubled since 2021.

Experts say overcrowding in boats makes crossings riskier . At least 84 people died while attempting to cross the Channel in 2024, according to the United Nations (UN).

When looking at the scale of small boats crossings, the number of these arrivals is about 5% of the size of total immigration into the UK from January 2025 to December 2025.

The government has pledged to “smash the gangs” behind these crossings in order to reduce the numbers.

People from Eritrea accounted for 18% of all arrivals from July 2025 to June 2026.

In the latest figures covering January 2025 to December 2025, at least 2,335 people who arrived by small boat were found to be potential victims of human trafficking or other forms of modern slavery, according to the Home Office.

Another 4,712 people were detected entering the UK without permission via other methods including hiding in vehicles, travelling on ferries or through airports from July 2025 to June 2026. This was down by 17% on the same period the previous year.

There are also individuals who arrive legally, for example via a work or study visa, and then overstay their limit.

The total number of people who live in the UK illegally after arriving legally is not known.

Asylum applications and hotels

An asylum seeker is someone who wants to be in the UK because they say they cannot live safely in their own country due to persecution or violence.

The government must house an asylum seeker if they cannot financially support themselves while their claim is being considered. There were 89,089 people in asylum accommodation as of June 2026.

About 18% of those people, 16,021, were in hotels. These are used when there is not enough shared housing available, such as houses of multiple occupation (HMOs) or former military sites .

The government has pledged to stop the use of hotels by 2029.

More people are in hotels across the south of England than elsewhere in the UK, while HMOs are more common in the north of England and Scotland.

A modern browser with JavaScript and a stable internet connection is required to view this interactive

Type in a postcode or the name of a local council below to see how many asylum seekers are housed in the area

A total of 85,891 people applied for asylum in the UK from July 2025 to June 2026. This was down by 21% on the same period in the previous year.

Most people who arrive in the UK by small boat claim asylum, but they were only 40% of all asylum seekers from July 2025 to June 2026.

The rest include people who arrived by other illegal means or who came to the UK legally and applied for asylum while holding, or just after holding, a valid visa.

It can take years for the government to decide whether someone should be granted asylum.

In June 2026, 40,168 people - across 32,401 asylum applications - were waiting for an initial decision. The number of people awaiting an initial decision was down by 56% on the previous year.

As of June 2026, a further 90,341 refused asylum applications were part of a second backlog, waiting the outcome of an appeal in the courts. This was up by 51% on the previous year.

Together, these initial decision and appeal cases form the government’s total asylum applications backlog, which it has pledged to clear .

Refugee status was granted in about 38% of asylum decisions made by the Home Office from July 2025 to June 2026.

About 39% of asylum appeal cases concluded between January 2026 to December 2026 resulted in a previous refusal decision being overturned.

Returns and deportations from the UK

The government requires people who are in the UK, but no longer have permission to live or work in the country, to leave.

This is called a return and can happen voluntarily or involuntarily.

People can lose the right to be in the UK for different reasons, such as a visa expiring, an asylum claim being refused, or by receiving a criminal conviction that results in deportation.

There were 40,605 returns from July 2025 to June 2026. This was up by 8% on the same period the previous year.

That number of returns is equivalent to about 6% of total emigration from the UK from January 2025 to December 2025.

Of all returns from July 2025 to June 2026:

5,962 had been convicted of a criminal offence 12,568 had lodged an asylum claim at some point 3,310 had arrived in the UK by small boat

People from India made up 27% of all returns from July 2025 to June 2026.

Up until September the UK was trialing a scheme with France to return people who arrived in the country on a small boat.

For every person the UK sent back to France, the UK accepted a number of asylum seekers.

This was called the "one in, one out" deal. As of 30 June 2026, 1,087 people were returned through this arrangement.

Returns can happen in different ways. "Enforced returns", which includes deportations, means the government arranges transport to return people to a different country. In some cases, people are escorted by officers.

All other returns are "voluntary". This means a person has agreed to leave and may receive government help with travel and other costs to help facilitate the return.

Some people classed as leaving the country voluntarily do so completely independently and without any government knowledge or involvement .

Independent returns made up 34% of the total from July 2025 to June 2026.

Visas for legal migration

Most people who come to the UK do so legally, after being granted a visa before they travel.

A visa gives someone permission to enter or stay in the UK for a specific purpose, such as work, study or joining family members.

There were 727,487 people who came to the UK via visas from July 2025 to June 2026, not including visitors or people transiting through the UK. This was down by 15% on the same period the previous year.

That does not mean all those people travelled to the UK, only that they were approved to do so.

The most common type of visa people came to the UK on was study, which made up 53% of all visa entries from July 2025 to June 2026.

People from China were the most common group to come to the UK on study visas, making up 23% of the total.

Together, people from China and India accounted for nearly half of all study visas. This has been the case for many years.

Migration to Europe

The EU and UK monitor the number of people crossing borders in the Mediterranean and English Channel by sea without permission.

There were 139,288 sea arrivals to the UK, Greece, Italy, Spain and Cyprus from August 2025 to July 2026.

Crossings to the UK accounted for about 22% of the combined total.

Sea arrivals into mainland Europe peaked in 2015, when the UN said more than a million people crossed the Mediterranean.

The top three countries with the most people claiming asylum from April 2025 to March 2026 were Spain with 133,795, Italy with 124,740 and France with 111,320.

The UK ranked at number five for asylum claims over the same period when compared with 26 other European countries with populations over one million.

When adjusted for population size, the UK ranks at number 10 for asylum applications per 100,000 people.

Net migration measures the overall change in a country’s population due to migration over a given period. It is everyone coming into the country (immigration) minus everyone who leaves (emigration).

The latest available data to compare the UK with other European nations is January 2024 to December 2024.

At that point, the countries with the biggest increase in their population were Spain with 626,000, Germany with 494,000 and the UK with 331,000, after taking into account the people who left the country, and those who arrived.

When adjusting for population size, the UK was in position 11 for increase in population due to migration, alongside 13 other European countries with comparable data per 100,000 residents.

Is the government meeting its pledges on illegal immigration and asylum? Published 26 February

Why do Channel migrants want to come to the UK? Published 9 July 2025

Find out more about people crossing the Channel in small boats Published 22 October 2025

Produced by: Rob England, Libby Rogers, Jess Carr, Aidan McNamee, John Walton, Becky Dale, Allison Shultes, Chris Kay, Steven Connor and Scott Jarvis.

Graphics by: Jez Frazer, Zoe Bartholomew and Joy Roxas

About the data

Figures from government and other official sources can be revised between publications. This page shows data as presented in the latest available release.

Immigration, emigration and net migration

*The net migration figure for the UK will not exactly equal immigration minus emigration because the Office for National Statistics (ONS) publishes it as a rounded number.

Immigration and emigration estimates , external from the ONS are updated twice a year.

Net migration figures use the internationally recognised definition of a long-term migrant: "A person who moves to a country other than that of their usual residence for at least a year."

Visas for legal migration

The total number of visa entries only includes visas that have been granted. It does not include visitor visas or transit visas, where the UK is not the final destination.

Visa figures record when permission was granted, not when or whether someone arrived in the UK.

If a person was granted more than one visa within the year shown, each visa is counted separately.

Work visas refer to new individuals granted permission, or extensions of existing permission. This includes categories such as seasonal work, health and care, domestic worker and youth mobility visas.

Study visas include all individuals sponsored by approved UK education providers, as well as those on short-term study visas.

Family visas allow someone to come to or remain in the UK to live with close family members already here. This includes joining a spouse, partner, child or parent, or coming to care for a relative.

The "Other" category includes visas outside work, study and family routes. This covers humanitarian schemes such as the Ukraine Sponsorship Scheme and the British National (Overseas) route. It also includes family permits for people from European Union or European Economic Area countries.

Asylum applications and accommodation

Home Office figures for asylum seekers in hotels are published under the category "contingency accommodation - hotel".

The number of people in all other forms of accommodation includes non-hotel contingency accommodation, as well as initial, dispersal and "other" accommodation.

To show how evenly accommodation is distributed, a scale compares each local authority's share of people in that type of accommodation with the UK-wide average for areas using the same accommodation type:

Less than half – more than 50% below the average share

Lower than – between 25% and 50% below the average share

About the same as – within 25% of the average share

Higher than – between 25% and 100% above the average share

More than double – more than 100% above the average share

Backlog figures for people waiting for an initial asylum decision include both main applicants and dependants.

Open appeals against refused asylum applications refer to individuals. Figures on appeals are published every three months by the Ministry of Justice, at a different time from other government asylum statistics. It also includes a small number of appeals against revocation of protection.

Small boat crossings and other irregular arrivals

Small boat crossing figures and the average number of people per boat are taken from the Home Office daily data , external .

Entering the UK without permission is an offence under immigration law , external , but asylum seekers are generally not prosecuted if they claim asylum on arrival. In some cases, people have been prosecuted alongside other offences, such as people smuggling or re-entering after deportation.

The International Organization for Migration (IOM) collects figures on people who have died , external or gone missing while crossing from mainland Europe to the UK. These reports are based on information from French and UK officials (such as police or coastguard) and media sources. The IOM considers them an undercount because there are no official statistics.

The figures may include people who died in the Channel itself, as well as those who died while travelling to a crossing point.

Data on modern slavery includes final decisions only. Modern slavery covers human trafficking, slavery, servitude and forced labour.

Figures for other entries without permission combine all recorded irregular arrivals that were not by small boat. This includes inadequately documented air arrivals, recorded detections at UK ports, and other recorded detections within the UK.

Returns and deportations

People who are denied entry at the border and then leave the UK are not included in the returns figures on this page.

Returns involving the government are grouped into three categories. Enforced returns (which include deportations) are cases where the Home Office requires someone to leave and arranges their removal, usually because they have no legal right to remain or following a criminal conviction.

Assisted voluntary returns are when someone agrees to leave the UK and receives government support, such as help with travel documents, flights or reintegration assistance.

Controlled voluntary returns are when someone leaves the UK voluntarily without being forcibly removed, but their departure is formally recorded by the Home Office.

Independent returns are referred to by the government as "other verified returns," and refer to individuals who have left the UK without

People returned after a criminal conviction include non-British citizens convicted in the UK of any criminal offence, or convicted abroad of a serious criminal offence.

UK migration compared with other countries

Sea arrival figures are taken from the UNHCR European sea arrivals dashboard and combined with UK Home Office small boat data.

Asylum application, immigration and emigration figures for European countries are the latest available data from Eurostat for: Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, Greece, Ireland, Italy, Netherlands, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, Czechia, Estonia, Hungary, Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Slovakia, Slovenia, Bulgaria, Romania, Norway, Switzerland and Croatia.

UK population figures are from ONS, National Records of Scotland and the Northern Ireland Statistics and Research Agency 2024 mid-year estimates. European population figures are from Eurostat as of 1 January 2024.

stories.title: Announcing Privacy Badger for Safari on macOS
stories.summary: Exciting news for Safari users: Privacy Badger is now available on Safari for macOS! You’ll need Safari version 26.5 or higher to use it. Whether you want to protect yourself from data brokers or just don’t want Big Tech profiting off your browsing data, Privacy Badger is here to help. More than 4 million people already use EFF’s free tracker-blocking extension to take a stand against online surveillance. Safari users can now join them and EFF in the fight for a better web. Install Privacy Badger Support the Fight Against Online Tracking Safari support has been one of Privacy Badger’s most requested features for years. Thanks to recent improvements in Safari's extension support, we’ve finally made it happen for Safari version 26.5 and higher. Privacy Badger is now available on all major desktop browsers. And before you ask, yes, we will look into supporting Safari for iOS once we've ironed out any issues on macOS. Why Install Privacy Badger on Safari? Most websites contain invisible tracking code that lets companies collect, share, and profit from your personal data. Some of those companies are data brokers that sell your information to anyone willing to pay. Creepy ads are just the tip of the iceberg when it comes to the harms of online tracking: Once your information enters the data broker ecosystem, it’s nearly impossible to know who buys it or what they’re doing with it. Privacy Badger blocks online trackers to prevent your browsing data from being used against you. Privacy Badger goes beyond Safari’s built-in privacy features to provide additional protection against online tracking. In its default browsing mode, Safari limits the information that trackers can access but still allows them to load. Privacy Badger blocks trackers from loading in the first place, preventing them from tracking you using techniques that bypass Safari’s protections. Privacy Badger works well by itself, and will continue to enhance your privacy when installed along side an ad blocker or with Safari’s Advanced settings to block trackers in all windows . Since Privacy Badger automatically learns to block trackers, Privacy Badger will block trackers that other tools don’t know about or choose not to block . For example, Privacy Badger blocks tracking from widgets like embedded tweets, comments sections, and video players. These widgets can share your data even if you never click…

Even after a guilty cull, my inbox is sitting at well over 7,000, but lately I’ve started subscribing to the Quentin Crisp theory of housework: why bother, when after four years or so you stop noticing the accumulating dust? Empty inboxes just fill up again anyway. In theory, email was supposed to save hours of meetings, phone calls and standing over photocopiers. Instead, we just spend hours deleting stuff people wouldn’t have bothered telling us if it had meant picking up the phone, but which they can now spam to their entire database at the click of a button.
